prompt: What is the race detector, physically?
hint: Think about what `go build -race` produces.

choices.text: A separate program that watches yours from outside
choices.why: There is no second program. The checking is compiled into yours.

choices.text: A second build of your own program
choices.why: Right. `-race` changes how the program is compiled, so the checks run inside it.

choices.text: A linter that reads the source without running it
choices.why: It needs the program to run: it reports races that happen, not races that could.

choices.text: A flag that makes goroutines take turns
choices.why: Goroutines still run in parallel under `-race`; that is how it sees them collide.

prompt: `cost` took 0.156 s plainly and 1.852 s built with `-race`. Roughly how many times slower was the race build? Give a whole number.
hint: 1.852 divided by 0.156.

prompt: The race build of `cost` was 12 times slower and held 9 times the memory. Why does the lesson say a server that mostly waits on a network would pay far less?
hint: What does the detector check, and how much of it does waiting do?

choices.text: The detector switches itself off during network calls
choices.why: It never switches off. Waiting is simply not something it has to check.

choices.text: Network code is compiled without `-race`
choices.why: `-race` applies to the whole program, standard library included.

choices.text: Waiting touches no memory, so there is little to check
choices.why: Right. `cost` does almost nothing but touch memory, which is the worst case.

choices.text: Servers run with `GORACE=halt_on_error=1`, which is cheaper
choices.why: That option decides when to stop after a report; it does not make checking cheaper.

prompt: Where does the lesson put the race detector? Choose all that apply.
hint: Who pays the cost, and who reads the report?

choices.text: `go test -race ./...` in CI on every change
choices.why: Yes, the single most useful line the course adds.

choices.text: Your own runs while you develop
choices.why: Yes. You pay the cost and you read the report.

choices.text: The binary shipped to every user
choices.why: Every user would pay the slowdown for a check that helps only whoever reads its output.

choices.text: A build without tests, run once before release
choices.why: One run sees only the races that happen in it. Tests that make goroutines meet, run on every change, see far more.

prompt: A program built with `-race` that found a race carries on running and, at the end, exits with status ___.
hint: Lesson 1 met the same number.

prompt: Put the parts of a race report in the order they are printed.
hint: The access that completed the race comes first.
items: the access that completed the race, with its stack
the previous access to the same address, with its stack
where each goroutine named was created
how many races were found, and status 66

prompt: In the `stats.go` report, the previous write's stack is `main.serve()` at line 22, then `main.main.gowrap1()` at line 15. What is line 15?
hint: `gowrap` is the runtime's wrapper around one kind of statement.

choices.text: The `go serve(s)` statement
choices.why: Right. The same line appears again as the goroutine's birthplace.

choices.text: The `fmt.Println` that read the counter
choices.why: That read is line 17, under the first block of the report.

choices.text: A second write to `s.served` inside `main`
choices.why: `main` writes nothing to the counter; line 15 only starts `serve`.

choices.text: The line where the program exited with status 66
choices.why: The exit status has no line in the source; the detector sets it when the program ends.

prompt: The plain run of `stats.go` printed `served so far: 10` and stopped normally. What does that tell you about the race?
hint: What did the plain run have, that the race run had in addition?

choices.text: That the race only exists in builds made with `-race`
choices.why: The race is in the source. `-race` is what makes it visible.

choices.text: Nothing: without the detector there is no symptom
choices.why: Right. That is why the detector exists; the plain run looked fine.

choices.text: That the read happened before every write
choices.why: The read came after about ten increments, unordered against them.

choices.text: That the counter is correct and the detector is wrong
choices.why: A plausible number is not evidence of order. Nothing synchronised the two goroutines.

prompt: A report's read stack ends in `runtime.mapaccess1_faststr` and never reaches your files, but the previous write names `tally.go:17`. What do you do?
hint: Both accesses were to the same address.

choices.text: Report a bug in Go's map implementation
choices.why: The runtime frames are where the map's memory is touched; the race is in the code that called it.

choices.text: Rerun until the read stack names a line, then fix
choices.why: Nothing is missing: one side naming your line is enough.

choices.text: Fix the map that line 17 updates
choices.why: Right. Same address, so both accesses are that `counts[w]++`.

choices.text: Ignore it, because a runtime frame means a false alarm
choices.why: The plain runs agreeing does not make the map safe; the detector saw two unordered accesses.

prompt: What does `GORACE=halt_on_error=1` change?
hint: `tally.go` had four reports without it.

choices.text: It makes the detector look for more kinds of race
choices.why: It changes nothing about what is detected, only what happens after the first report.

choices.text: It turns the race build back into a plain build
choices.why: `GORACE` is read by the detector inside a race build; a plain build has no detector to read it.

choices.text: The program stops at the first report
choices.why: Right. One report is easier to read, and you fix them one at a time anyway.

choices.text: It hides reports that point inside the runtime
choices.why: The one report it printed started in `runtime.mapaccess2_faststr`.

prompt: Match each shared thing with the fix the lesson chose for it.
hint: Ask what is shared, and how many steps an update takes.

pairs.left: a value handed from a worker to a collector

prompt: Why was `tally.go` given a mutex rather than an atomic?
hint: What does `counts[w]++` do to a map?

choices.text: Atomics are slower than a mutex
choices.why: Speed was not the reason. An atomic cannot make several steps on a map look like one.

choices.text: Each update is several steps on one structure, done as one
choices.why: Right: look up, add, store, perhaps grow. A mutex makes the sequence one step to everyone else.

choices.text: The map was too large for an atomic
choices.why: Size is not the issue; an atomic type holds one value, and a map update is not one operation.

choices.text: `sync/atomic` cannot be imported in a `main` package
choices.why: `stats.go`, a `main` package, imported it a section earlier.

prompt: `collect.go` was fixed with no lock, no atomic and no channel. Why is writing `results[i]` from a thousand goroutines not a race?
hint: A race needs the same memory.

choices.text: Writes to a slice are atomic in Go
choices.why: They are not; `append` raced on that same slice a moment earlier.

choices.text: `wg.Wait` orders the goroutines against each other
choices.why: `wg.Wait` orders the goroutines against main, not against each other.

choices.text: `make` locks the slice for the rest of the program
choices.why: `make` only allocates. Nothing is locked.

choices.text: Each goroutine writes a different element of the slice
choices.why: Right. Different elements are different memory, so no two accesses meet.

prompt: After the mutex went into `tally.go`, the program printed exactly the map it printed before. What had the fix changed?
hint: Was the old answer right by construction?

choices.text: It is right by construction now, and the detector agrees
choices.why: Right, and the detector, run again, agrees.

choices.text: Nothing, so the mutex can be removed
choices.why: Without it the detector reported four races; the plain runs were right by luck.

choices.text: The order in which the words are printed
choices.why: `fmt` prints a map sorted by key either way.

choices.text: The program now runs on one processor
choices.why: A mutex does not change `GOMAXPROCS`; it orders the accesses to the map.

prompt: A type keeps a `count` and a `total` that must always change together. A colleague makes both `atomic.Int64`. What is still wrong?
hint: What can a reader see between the two updates?

choices.text: Nothing, because each field is now safe
choices.why: Each field is safe on its own; the pair is not.

choices.text: `atomic.Int64` cannot hold a total
choices.why: It holds any 64-bit integer. The problem is the gap between two updates.

choices.text: Between the two Adds, a reader sees a half-made pair
choices.why: Right. Two values that move together are a structure, and a structure needs a mutex.

choices.text: The detector will report every `Add` as a race
choices.why: Atomic operations are synchronised and the detector knows it; it reports nothing, which is why this one is subtle.

prompt: `go test ./cache` and `go test -count=5 ./cache` both passed on the unfixed `Cache`. Why did the checks on the answers not catch the race?
hint: What was the risk: a wrong answer, or something else?

choices.text: The tests did not call `Get` from several goroutines
choices.why: `TestGetFromManyGoroutines` did exactly that, six at once.

choices.text: The risk was two map writes at once
choices.why: Right. Only the detector sees unordered accesses that happened to give the right answer.

choices.text: `-count=5` reused a cached result
choices.why: `-count` forces the tests to run; the output showed a fresh time, not `(cached)`.

choices.text: `strings.ToUpper` is too fast to race
choices.why: Speed changes how often the accesses overlap, never whether they are ordered.

prompt: Under `go test -race`, what turns a race report into a failing test?
hint: Read the end of `race.log`.

choices.text: A `t.Errorf` the test author has to write
choices.why: No assertion was added; the test failed with the same code that passed.

choices.text: The testing package fails it by itself
choices.why: Right, so CI goes red without anybody reading the report.

choices.text: Exit status 66 from the test binary
choices.why: The go command reported FAIL and the shell saw 1; it is the test's verdict that matters.

choices.text: A panic inside `Get`
choices.why: `Get` never panicked; the answers were right every time.

prompt: Why would running the `cache` package's own code with `-race`, without `TestGetFromManyGoroutines`, find nothing?
hint: The detector reports races that happen in the run it watches.

choices.text: Packages that are not `main` cannot be built with `-race`
choices.why: `go test -race ./cache` built that package with the detector.

choices.text: The mutex hides the race
choices.why: The unfixed `Cache` had no mutex.

choices.text: No code in it ever runs concurrently
choices.why: Right. A test has to make the goroutines meet before the detector can see them collide.

choices.text: `TestGet` runs first and warms the cache
choices.why: Each test makes its own `Cache` with `New`; nothing carries over.

prompt: The fix holds the mutex for the whole of `Get`, including the slow `lookup`. What does that cost?
hint: Two goroutines want two different keys.

choices.text: A race between `lookup` and `seen`
choices.why: The detector ran twenty times and reported nothing.

choices.text: A deadlock when the same key is asked twice
choices.why: The second call waits for the first to unlock and then finds the answer remembered.

choices.text: Lookups of different keys wait in line
choices.why: Right. Correct first; lessons 8 and 9 show how to hold the lock for less time.

choices.text: Twice the memory of the unfixed version
choices.why: A mutex is a few bytes; the cost is waiting, not memory.

prompt: Put the steps of handling a race report in order.
hint: Diagnose before touching the code, and prove the fix after.
items: read the two accesses and their lines
say what is shared and how it is updated
choose an atomic, a mutex, ownership or a channel
run the detector again over the same tests

prompt: A handler increments `hits[path]++` in a package-level map on every request. Tests call the handler once each and pass under `-race`. In production the server sometimes dies with a map error. Which test would have shown the race?
hint: Section 05: make the goroutines meet.

choices.text: The same tests with `-count=100`
choices.why: Repeating one call at a time never puts two goroutines on the map together.

choices.text: Several goroutines calling it at once, with `-race`
choices.why: Right. That is the shape of `TestGetFromManyGoroutines`.

choices.text: A test without `-race`, so the race is not slowed down
choices.why: Without the detector a race is visible only by luck, as `tally.go` showed.

choices.text: A test that checks the final count of `hits` is right
choices.why: A right count proves nothing; `tally.go` printed right counts with four races in it.

prompt: The command that runs every test of every package in a module with the detector watching is `go test ___ ./...`.
hint: The flag this lesson is named after.
